name: Acre
summary_text: Brazil's uniform national framework applies with no state-specific law or enforcement pattern documented. In ANTRA's annual state-by-state killings dossier, no killings were found recorded in Acre for 2024. Acre is among the least populous federation units, so a single case moves its rate enormously - the recorded zero carries little evidential weight. No deviation material enough to treat apart from the national position was found.

sources.claim_summary: Wikipedia overview of LGBTQ rights in Brazil: the national legal timeline - recognition of same-sex unions and marriage (STF 2011/CNJ 2013), adoption, discrimination protections, gender identity and expression (the March 2018 rulings allowing name/gender-marker change without surgery), conversion therapy, military service and blood donation, plus a section listing non-binary marker rules by federative unit. Framework is national; state-level variation is not covered by this page.

sources.title: Brazil | Outright International
sources.claim_summary: International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2012 -> March 2026 file): same-sex relations legal throughout the country; legal gender recognition possible by self-determination; a 2019 Supreme Court ruling prohibits discrimination and hate crimes on SOGI grounds; marriage equality since 2013 with active repeal efforts in Congress; Brazil continues to have one of the highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, particularly trans people; 3,000+ openly LGBTQ candidates ran in the 2024 municipal elections; a 2025 Superior Court of Justice ruling allows nonbinary civil-registry amendments; executive pro-rights vs a conservative legislature generating a surge of anti-LGBTIQ proposals.

Brazilian law-firm guide to LGBTQ+ legal rights for expats (updated April 2026): protections were established by the judiciary (STF/CNJ) rather than statute - same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality, joint adoption, name and gender-marker change without surgery, and criminalisation of homophobia/transphobia as equivalent to racism; major cities broadly welcoming with legal infrastructure accustomed to same-sex marriages and name changes; the guide states smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction, 'though the legal rights are identical nationwide'.
